newsitem.title: USA: CBOT wheat futures end higher on weather concerns.
newsitem.headline: CBOT wheat futures end higher on weather concerns.

text.p: CBOT wheat futures closed higher with new contract highs set in the deferred months, an eight month high notched in the May, and new crop July setting a sessionm high close to its one year high, traders said.
Concerns about harsh weather in several wheat regions worldwide boosted the market, but trading was volatile and the May contract swung in a 15-1/2-cent trading range.

"Flooding in the Northern Plains is very bad and there was very little relief in Europe over the weekend," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter. "There was a little rain in southern France but not much and the forecasts are dry."

Nearby May reached a session high of $4.49 per bushel, an eight-month high. The $4.49 level was last reached by the May on August 13. The active new crop July contract was closing in on its one year high and traded at $4.59 per bushel. July last saw that level on May 2, 1996. It reached $4.60 on April 15, 1996 and set its contract high of $4.65 on April 11, 1996. September set a contract high of $4.63, above the previous high of $4.50 set Friday.
Wheat closed one to eight cents per bushel higher, with May up 2-1/2 at $4.39-1/2. New crop July closed 2-3/4 cents per bushel higher at $4.47-1/4.

The CBOT wheat market, while closing higher, was well below the day's highs and the KCBT hard red winter market ended lower in the nearby contracts. Some traders said the wheat markets were pressured late by a report U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said there was no freeze damage to the Kansas wheat crop north of Interstate 70.
"When the Secretary of Agriculture says there's no damage to the Kansas wheat crop north of 1-70, that means something to the market," a trader said.

But the market also remained wary of flooding in the Northern U.S. spring wheat growing region and on the variety of opinions about the extent of the freeze damage a week ago in the U.S. Great Plains hard red winter wheat crop. There were escalating concerns about dry weather in European wheat growing areas.

North Dakota Democratic Congressman Earl Pomeroy Sunday said about 1.7 million acres of North Dakota cropland were under water due to flooding and much of that acreage will not go into agricultural production this growing season. North Dakota, especially the Red River Valley region separating North Dakota and Minnesota, is a key U.S. spring wheat growing area.

The concern about dry weather in European wheat areas extended from France the key high quality milling wheat producer into the mainly feed wheat producing area of England. Dry weather in Spain also was cited.
Early wheat was turning yellow in parched fields in eastern England and Europeans were puzzling about the wheat following a dry spring in the West and bitter cold in the East, European sources said.
"Crops are starting to yellow, especially the late drilled ones," one co-op manager in the East England area said. "With no prospect of rain, people are getting concerned."

The impact of the dry weather was most directly felt by farmers who report real signs of damage to cereals in Britain and Spain, European trade sources said. French weather forecasters, officials and farmers have so far refused to talk of a full blown drought, despite irrigation bans in some areas after the prolonged dry spell.
Also there still hasn't been a definitive statement about the extent of freeze damage that occurred in the U.S. Great Plains hard red winter wheat growing region just over a week ago.
Crop specialists have said the freeze may have sliced more than 100 million bushels from the Kansas wheat crop and severe losses in Oklahoma also were likely.
The market also took note of potential cold weather in Kansas again late this week and China was mentioned as another potential troublesome spot.
"There's talk of a freeze in China and maybe another chance for a freeze in the U.S. late this week," a trader said.

In wheat futures, USA Trading sold seven million bushels of July and bought two million July, traders said. Lee B. Stern and Co, Refco Inc and LIT America each bought between one million and two million bushels of July, traders said. Griffin Trading, LFG Futures and Cargill Inc each sold one million bushels of July, traders said.
Wheat futures volume was estimated by the CBOT at 37,000 contracts, above the 33,295 traded Friday.

In wheat options, FIMAT Futures bought 1,500 July $4.00 puts and sold 1,500 July $4.30 puts at eight to nine cents, traders said. FIMAT also bought 1,000 July $4.00 puts and sold 1,000 July $4.20 puts at 5-1/4 to 5-3/4 cents, traders said.
Wheat options volume was estimated at 15,000 contracts, below the 18,149 traded Friday.
